newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary panel meets Tuesday on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary panel meets Tuesday on single currency.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee will meet on Tuesday to move foreward on a budget stability pact for countries joining a single currency in 1999, monetary officials said on Monday.

The group, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, will also focus on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) that links the single currency, the euro, to currencies outside monetary union.
Rounding out the discussion will be the legal underpinnings of monetary union, with an emphasis on how a legal framework for the euro can be obtained in advance of the 1999 start date.
"It's more of the same," said one source familiar with the group's deliberations.

Coming on the heels of an informal gathering of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin last month, the committee will have to sort out a number of unresolved technical details in each of the three areas.
STABILITY PACT -- It is now agreed there will be such a pact which fines governments running budget deficits above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
There remains, however, the rather difficult task of defining the economic circumstances under which a government could avoid sanctions should its deficit rise above the three percent threshold.

Many officials believe it will be a struggle to find agreement on a precise and quantitative definition of so-called exceptional and temporary economic circumstances -- in other words, a sharp economic downturn.
Another issue concerns the time period between when a government is cited as having an excessive deficit and when it would actually have to pay a fine.
A consensus appears to be forming around nine months, although Germany is still apparently arguing for a shorter gap of six to seven months.
The issue is credibility. Many officials believe there is a need to give an offending government sufficient time to ensure that its deficit-correcting measures actually pass through parliament.
EU governments operating with broad coalition partners might need more time than those with near absolute majorities.

Lastly, there is debate over the level of fines a government would face, although many seem to be leaning towards the European Commission's proposal -- an initial 0.2 or 0.3 percent of a country's GDP, followed by 0.1 percent of total output for every percentage point above the three percent level.
A maximum ceiling of 0.5 percent of output is also proposed.
ERM II - All members accept the principle that the single currency will be the anchor of a revamped ERM with broad -- probably 15 percent -- fluctuation bands for those outside.

There would be the opportunity, however, for non-EMU countries to arrange alternative bi-lateral trading ranges amongst themselves and there is a broad acceptance that as a country improves its budgetary performance, a reduction in its trading bands is possible.

What remains unspecified -- and might for some time to come -- are the obligations a European Central Bank has in supporting a non-EMU currency. There is a strong desire to place limits on such intervention.
The ECB should also have some authority in initiating parity changes of outside currencies should they come under speculative attack, but exactly how much is unclear.

LEGAL ISSUES -- There is agreement that the most urgent legal points of concern for financial markets -- the single currency's name; the continuity of contracts after January 1, 1999; a one-for-one conversion rate between and Ecu-basket of currencies and the euro, and a rule for sub-divisions of the euro -- should be brought into legal force quickly.
The monetary committee will consider a Commission plan on how to do this within the bounds of the Maastricht treaty.
